_note: Completed from the participant-pack template. If the template in the arena differs in field names, replace this file with the official one and carry these values across before submitting.

stack.backend: One optional server route (app/api/chat) that holds the Gemini key server-side. The solver, the rules and the board are entirely client-side; the four scored requirements work with the route absent.
stack.database: Optional Supabase table for publishing a day so others can open it. Not used by any scored requirement; without it, days are kept in the browser.
stack.map: Leaflet 1.9.4 (BSD-2-Clause), OpenStreetMap tiles via CARTO, attributed on the map
stack.assistant: Two layers: a deterministic grammar (lib/console.ts) first, then Gemini via app/api/chat for anything it does not recognise. The model may propose one command from a fixed list; the browser re-validates every id and runs it through the same handlers the buttons use, so it still passes checkFeasible.

data_source.additional: lib/seed.ts — one hand-built demo day, 12 technicians and 40 jobs, invented data

requirements.requirement: At least 12 technicians with skills, shift start and end times and a home area; at least 30 jobs with an area, a required skill, a duration and a customer time window.
requirements.where: data/P11_route_shift_public.json via lib/cases.ts; lib/seed.ts; lib/caseFile.ts for days written by the user
requirements.evidence: 26 selectable days. Published cases carry 12-16 technicians and 30-40 jobs each. Test: 'every case meets the stated minimums'. A day can also be written by hand: the app imports and exports the same schema 2.1 JSON, validated field by field before anything loads.

requirements.requirement: Assignment method respecting the hard rules — right skill, inside shift hours, inside the customer time window including area-to-area travel — then improve one stated goal.
requirements.objective: Minimise total travel time across all technicians, with jobs placed as the primary term.
requirements.evidence: Across all 26 days: 858 of 932 jobs placed and 9224 minutes of travel, against a random feasible baseline of 821.9 jobs and 25178 minutes — 63.4% less travel. Reproduce with `npm run stats`. On PUB-01: 34 of 37 placed, 580 min vs 873 min random.

requirements.requirement: Show the day plan as a timeline per technician with jobs, travel gaps and idle time, plus a list of jobs that could not be assigned and the exact rule that blocked each one.
requirements.evidence: Three visually distinct block types per lane, explained in the legend. Blocked panel names the rule, the shortfall in minutes and the closest technician, and expands to the verdict for every technician. Every one of the 26 days has 2-5 blocked jobs, so the list is never empty. Tests: 'the timeline accounts for every minute of a technician shift', 'the blocked list names a rule and a human reason for every unplaced job'. A second view draws the same plan as one route per technician on a real map of Dhaka (Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles; lib/geo.ts holds approximate area centroids for drawing only — the travel table stays the sole authority on distance). The map also weights each leg by its travel time and names the three costliest, plays the day back so every technician can be seen at their real position at any minute, and — for a blocked job — draws every qualified technician with the distance that made the rule inevitable.

requirements.requirement: Let the dispatcher move a job to another technician by hand and immediately show whether that move breaks a hard rule, naming the rule.
requirements.evidence: Two surfaces share one verdict function. Dragging a job shows, for every lane, whether it may land and the exact rule if not — before the pointer is released; the dropdown lists the same verdicts and is the keyboard route. Both call previewMoves(), which asks checkFeasible. All 25 published scripted moves are rejections spanning SKILL_MISMATCH, WINDOW_MISSED and OVERLAPS_JOB, and each is named correctly. Tests: "every published scripted manual move gets a named verdict", "every move previewMoves calls legal really is legal", "every move previewMoves refuses names the rule that refuses it".

hard_rules.name: NO_RETURN_TIME
hard_rules.reason: The published P11 format note states 'the travel table is authoritative and symmetric; no return home is required'. The rule is implemented, unit-tested and switchable in the UI, and the crafted demo day enables it.

ambiguity_calls: A job must START inside the customer time window; overrunning the window end is allowed. Arriving early is allowed and shown as idle time.
Travel to the first job of the day starts from the technician's home area, and the shift clock starts then.
Returning to the home area before shift end is implemented as NO_RETURN_TIME but is OFF by default, because the published format note says no return home is required.

bonus_features_attempted.feature: A technician calls in sick and their remaining jobs are redistributed
bonus_features_attempted.where: lib/replan.ts (callInSick), Sick button on every technician lane
bonus_features_attempted.evidence: The lane is cleared and every lifted job is either rehomed or listed in the blocked list with its rule. Work already under way is never taken off them. 3 tests.

bonus_features_attempted.feature: An emergency job is added mid-day and only the jobs not yet started are replanned
bonus_features_attempted.evidence: Jobs already started at the set clock keep their exact technician, start and finish; everything else is replanned with the emergency offered first. 3 tests.

bonus_features_attempted.feature: A score for the plan, and a manual plan compared against the generated one
bonus_features_attempted.where: lib/score.ts, the comparison strip in components/board/Header.tsx
bonus_features_attempted.evidence: 10 points per job placed minus 1 point per 10 minutes of driving. Once the plan is edited by hand the header shows jobs, travel and score against the generated plan, with a restore button. 1 test.

bonus_features_attempted.feature: Drag and drop a job between technicians
bonus_features_attempted.where: @dnd-kit/core in components/board/TechnicianLane.tsx and DispatchBoard.tsx, verdicts from lib/moves.ts
bonus_features_attempted.evidence: Picking up a job marks every lane with whether it may land and the rule if not, before the drop. Dropping on the blocked panel takes the job off the board. The dropdown remains as the keyboard route and shares the same verdict function. 5 tests.

bonus_features_attempted.feature: A dispatcher console — type a command in plain English and the board does it
bonus_features_attempted.where: lib/console.ts (grammar and answers), components/board/Console.tsx, runCommand in DispatchBoard.tsx
bonus_features_attempted.evidence: Understands move, assign, unassign, sick, emergency, solve, clear, restore, load a case, switch view, toggle the return-home rule, and answers why a job is blocked, who could take it, who is busiest and the day summary. Anything the grammar does not recognise goes to Gemini through a server route that keeps the key out of the browser; the model may propose one command, which is re-validated against the day and run through the same handlers the buttons use. Every plan-changing path still goes through checkFeasible. 23 tests on the grammar, including one asserting every example in the help text actually parses.

verification.tests: npm test — 127 tests, covering one case per hard rule, all 25 published cases, route legality, timeline contiguity, blocked-list coverage, the better-than-random claim, server-rendered board markup, and all three bonus features
verification.stats: npm run stats — per-case optimised vs random comparison

third_party: See LICENSES.md — dependencies, the create-next-app scaffold, shadcn/ui, fonts, the event-issued case file, and the OpenStreetMap/CARTO map tiles loaded at runtime.
known_limitations: Insertion does not ripple: a job that would fit if a later job slid is refused, which keeps every promised window intact but leaves some placeable work unplaced.
The solver is greedy plus a bounded local search, not an exact method; the 200-iteration caps are reached on larger cases.
Manual moves cannot be undone; re-solving rebuilds the plan.
Responsive down to a laptop screen only, as the brief allows. Not designed for a phone.
No persistence: reloading returns to the unsolved state.
